clinicalPearls: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply, while acids typically cause coagulative necrosis with an eschar that may limit depth, though both can be severe
The absence of visible oral burns does not exclude significant oesophageal or gastric injury, so symptoms guide assessment more than mouth findings
Drooling, stridor, dysphagia, odynophagia, chest or abdominal pain and vomiting suggest significant injury requiring urgent evaluation
Do not induce emesis, give neutralising agents or activated charcoal, and avoid blind nasogastric tube placement, as these can worsen injury or obscure endoscopy
Airway assessment takes priority, as laryngeal or supraglottic oedema can progress rapidly to obstruction
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within an appropriate early window grades injury and guides prognosis and feeding decisions
Signs of perforation or mediastinitis, such as severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema or peritonism, mandate urgent surgical involvement
Late oesophageal strictures and an increased long-term risk of oesophageal carcinoma warrant structured follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Caustic agents injure tissue on contact according to their pH, concentration, volume and contact time. Strong alkalis produce liquefactive necrosis, saponifying fats and dissolving proteins so injury extends deeply into and potentially through the oesophageal wall. Strong acids cause coagulative necrosis, forming a superficial eschar that can limit but not prevent deep penetration, and often preferentially injure the stomach. Tissue damage evolves over days through inflammation, then granulation and fibrosis, which underlies later stricture formation, while full-thickness injury risks perforation, mediastinitis and peritonitis.
additionalDifferentials: Thermal burn of the upper aerodigestive tract
Systemic toxicity from a co-ingested agent
additionalInvestigations: Early upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to grade mucosal injury
Erect chest and abdominal imaging, or contrast/computed tomography, to detect perforation and mediastinal or peritoneal air
Arterial blood gas and lactate to assess systemic acid-base disturbance and tissue injury
Full blood count, renal and liver function and coagulation
Blood group and crossmatch if surgical intervention is anticipated
Airway assessment with laryngoscopy where upper airway injury is suspected
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness or drooling indicating airway compromise
Severe chest or abdominal pain, subcutaneous emphysema or peritonism suggesting perforation
Haematemesis or signs of significant gastrointestinal haemorrhage
High-grade circumferential or deep injury on endoscopy
reference.prognosis: Minor mucosal injury usually heals without sequelae, but deep circumferential burns frequently lead to oesophageal strictures requiring dilatation, and severe transmural injury carries substantial morbidity and mortality; there is a lasting increased risk of oesophageal malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal oral examination excludes serious distal injury
Attempting to neutralise the agent or induce vomiting, worsening tissue damage
Giving activated charcoal, which is ineffective and obscures endoscopic assessment
Delaying airway management until obstruction is established
Failing to arrange follow-up for stricture and malignancy surveillance
references: UpToDate: Caustic esophageal injury in adults
management: Prioritise airway assessment and protection, with early intubation for laryngeal or supraglottic oedema and stridor
Avoid induced emesis, neutralising agents, activated charcoal and blind nasogastric tube placement, which worsen injury or obscure endoscopy
Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluid resuscitation and analgesia
Early upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to grade mucosal injury and guide feeding and prognosis
Proton pump inhibitor acid suppression to support mucosal healing
Emergency surgical resection for transmural necrosis, perforation, mediastinitis or peritonitis
Endoscopic dilatation for subsequent stricture formation
Long-term surveillance endoscopy given the lasting increased risk of oesophageal malignancy
